summary: The bad() method uses the non-short-circuit bitwise AND operator (`&`) in the guard `(myString != null) & (myString.length() > 0)`. With `&`, both operands are always evaluated, so `myString.length()` is dereferenced even when `myString` is null, causing a NullPointerException. Switching to the logical short-circuit AND operator (`&&`) makes the null check act as a guard: when `myString` is null the right operand is never evaluated, eliminating the null dereference while preserving the length-check behavior for valid non-null strings.
